source.text:
Peeking inflates false positives. Miller's worst case: testing after every observation and stopping at first p<0.05 turns a nominal 5% false positive rate into 26.1%. His peeking table: to get a true 5% you need reported significance of 2.9% (1 peek), 2.2% (2), 1.8% (3), 1.4% (5), 1.0% (10). Etsy Engineering (Code as Craft, October 3 2018) put numbers on it with a true null at a 50% baseline and alpha 0.10: "if we do peek and we check the significance level at every observation, then after 500 observations, there is over a 50% chance of incorrectly stating that treatment is different than the control." Kohavi and Sonnet's practical number: running two weeks then checking daily for two more weeks pushes a 5% error rate to about 17%.

Sequential methods legitimise looking early:

mSPRT (mixture sequential probability ratio test): Johari, Koomen, Pekelis, Walsh, "Always Valid Inference" (arXiv 2015; Operations Research 2022). Produces always-valid p-values valid at any stopping time. Used by Optimizely, Uber, Netflix, Amplitude.

GAVI (generalisation of always-valid inference): Howard et al. 2021 confidence sequences. Used by Eppo.

Group sequential design (GST) with alpha spending: Lan-DeMets 1983. Used by Spotify, which prefers GST over AVI for its power advantage in batch-analysed settings (Spotify Engineering, March 2023).

Corrected-alpha approach (CAA): used by Statsig. Tradeoff: always-valid methods let you stop any time but cost power (wider intervals) versus a correctly-sized fixed test. Spotify's guidance: if you can estimate the expected sample size well, GST is more powerful; if you cannot, always-valid is safer.

Minimum runtime: run at least one full week, and in practice two, to cover the weekly business cycle (Kohavi, "Five Puzzling Outcomes"). Weekends convert differently from weekdays; buyers differ by day. Two weeks captures one full cycle of returning visitors.

Novelty and primacy effects. Novelty: a change gets a temporary bump because it is new; the effect decays. Primacy: existing users are primed to the old design and the new one underperforms at first, then recovers. Both are threats to external validity (Kohavi, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments). Diagnose by plotting daily effect over time and by comparing first-exposure vs repeat-exposure conversion for the variant. Kohavi's surprising finding: most suspected novelty/primacy effects are actually statistical artifacts of early, noisy cumulative deltas, not real trends.

4. low-traffic methods with thresholds

The governing principle: below the A/B threshold, the job shifts from proving things statistically to learning fast and cheaply. Test bigger, not more.

Methods and when each applies:

Bold, big-swing A/B tests. Below about 100,000 visitors/month, default to differentiated changes with a target effect of 10-20%+, not tweaks (aiformarketing.news; VWO concedes low-traffic sites should make big changes). One bold homepage test teaches more than 10 micro-tests on low-traffic category pages (SplitBase).

Test on higher-traffic pages. Concentrate tests where the traffic is: homepage, top product pages, cart. Do not test low-traffic category pages.

Sequential before/after with honest error bars. Only when parallel testing is impossible and you can hold external conditions constant. Best for large structural changes. Treat as weak evidence.

Holdouts and pre/post with controls. Re-test any surprising large winner with a holdout before banking the revenue.

Qualitative research first. Session replay, surveys, user testing to generate strong hypotheses when you cannot run many tests.

Micro-conversions (add-to-cart, begin-checkout) as primary metric. They are more frequent so they power faster, but the risk is real: a lift in add-to-cart may not carry through to purchase or revenue. Use them as a leading indicator, keep purchase/revenue as guardrails.

A/B/n and bandits: only at 3,000+ orders/month.

5. Bayesian vs frequentist in practice

Frequentist: controls long-run error rates via pre-set sample size, fixed alpha, analysis plan. Outputs p-values and confidence intervals. Pros: explicit error-rate contract, forces upfront MDE/sample discipline, reproducible across tools (a z-test is a z-test). Cons: p-values are widely misinterpreted, the 0.05 cliff is artificial, fixed sample is rigid, peeking silently breaks it.

Bayesian: computes posterior probabilities given data and a prior. Outputs "probability B beats A" and expected loss. Pros: intuitive for stakeholders, gives magnitude and risk, credible intervals mean what people think. Cons: priors are subjective and usually hidden by vendors; "probability to be best" can mislead without a loss function.

How tools report:

VWO SmartStats: Bayesian, Beta-Binomial conjugate with Monte Carlo, reports probability-to-beat-baseline and expected loss.

Optimizely Stats Engine: frequentist with mSPRT always-valid p-values plus False Discovery Rate control instead of raw Type I control.

AB Tasty: Bayesian by preference.

Eppo: Bayesian with shrinkage plus GAVI sequential.

Statsig: sequential always-valid (corrected-alpha).

GrowthBook: both frequentist and Bayesian, plus sequential.

The two big pitfalls to flag: (1) Bayesian is not immune to peeking. Alex Molas (October 30 2025) simulated this: peeking after every 100 observations and stopping when P(A>B)>0.95 pushed the false positive rate to about 80%. A fixed posterior threshold does not control frequentist error under optional stopping. (2) Most commercial "Bayesian" tools use uninformative/flat priors, which makes them mathematically close to frequentist tests but with less transparency about what prior was used. If you cannot state the prior, you cannot fully interpret or reproduce the result (Convert.com; dripagency.de).

6. common invalidations

Sample ratio mismatch (SRM): the observed traffic split differs from the designed split (e.g. 50/50 comes back 50.3/49.7). Detect with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test on the randomisation unit (users, not page views). Kohavi: about 6% of Microsoft experiments show SRM. If SRM is present the result is biased and should not be trusted until the cause is found. Kameleoon flags SRM at p<0.001. Test early and often; it is easy to run in a spreadsheet.

Flicker (FOOC, Flash of Original Content): in client-side tests the original page renders briefly before JavaScript swaps in the variant. GrowthBook docs: "this flickering can lead to inaccurate or unreliable test results... rather counterintuitively, flickering may have a positive effect on the results, sometimes the flashing may draw a user's attention to that variation, and cause an inflation in the effect." So flicker both hurts UX and biases the read. Mitigate with anti-flicker snippets (hide body until variant ready), synchronous script loading high in the head, or server-side testing. Anti-flicker snippets have a cost: they hide the page for up to 3-4 seconds by default and slow initial load (DebugBear; Andy Davies).

Bot traffic: bots create skew and SRM; filter them (Kohavi/Sonnet).

Tracking breakage: if the pixel/event breaks mid-test, the experiment is invalid. This is the one MEA concern that belongs here.

Seasonality and promotions overlapping a test: a sale or holiday during one variant's window confounds before/after tests and can distort even parallel tests if it changes the visitor mix.

Multiple comparisons: testing many metrics or segments inflates false positives. With one decision metric error is 5%, two metrics about 10%, three about 14% (Kohavi/Sonnet). Correct with Bonferroni or FDR.

Novelty effects: see section 3.

Segment fishing: slicing results after the fact until you find a "winning" segment is p-hacking. Pre-register segments.

Stopping early: see peeking, section 3.

Twyman's law: any figure that looks interesting or surprising is usually wrong. A 364% lift is more likely an instrumentation bug, SRM, or contamination than a discovery (Kohavi). This is the anchor rule for auditing case studies.

7. variance reduction: CUPED

CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data), Deng, Xu, Kohavi, Walker, Microsoft 2013. Uses pre-experiment data (usually the same metric measured before the test) as a covariate to strip out variance not caused by the treatment. Adjusted estimator stays unbiased but has lower variance, so you reach significance faster or detect smaller effects at the same sample. Optimizely's glossary: can cut sample requirements 30-50% for metrics with strong correlation to historical behaviour. Now default-on in several tools (Datadog, Optimizely) and used by Netflix, Airbnb, Booking.

Practicality for DTC: mixed. CUPED needs pre-experiment data keyed to the same user, which means logged-in users or stable device IDs. For a DTC brand where most checkout traffic is new or not logged in, the pre-period covariate is often missing or weakly correlated, so the variance reduction is smaller. The clearest evidence of the ceiling: Jin, Ba and colleagues at LinkedIn ("Towards Optimal Variance Reduction in Online Controlled Experiments", arXiv 2110.13406) ran CUPED on n=400,000 feed members and found it "reduces 15.91% of variance compared to the diff-in-mean estimator", limited because "member's revenue is a volatile metric whose autocorrelation across different time periods is weak." Verdict: worth turning on if your platform offers it and you have returning identified users; not a magic fix for a brand with mostly new, anonymous traffic. Simpler cousins that help ecommerce more: pick a proportion metric instead of a raw revenue mean, and winsorize (cap) outlier orders.

8. multi-armed bandits vs A/B tests

A/B test: two periods, explore (split evenly) then exploit (ship winner). Best when you need a clean, high-confidence causal read before a lasting change: redesigns, pricing, navigation, checkout. Gives a defensible answer and a measured effect size.
